title: Gatherings that last (Avot 4:11)
hook: a group chat splitting into side chats: Yochanan the sandal-maker says every gathering for heaven's sake will endure
tomorrow: you embarrassed someone younger in front of everyone. now what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: one good deed, one advocate; one wrong, one accuser. Make an advocate. Today, the same mishnah, a new voice.

First the main group chat goes quiet. Then the side chats start. Two people who were friends last month now leave a room when the other walks in. Somebody says: we need a meeting. And somebody else says: we need a meeting so I can tell them exactly what they did. Same word, two different meetings. Which one actually lasts? A sage who made sandals for a living answered that.
screen: `THE MAIN CHAT GOES QUIET.` → `WE NEED A MEETING.` → `WHICH ONE LASTS?`

segments.voice: His name in the Mishnah is Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, Yochanan the sandal-maker, a sage known by his trade. Here's his saying, in plain words. Every gathering that is for the sake of heaven will endure in the end. And one that is not for the sake of heaven will not endure in the end. For the sake of heaven, l'shem shamayim, is the key. It doesn't mean the meeting has to be about God, or held in a synagogue. It means the gathering is for something bigger than the people in it. Not for my side winning. Not for being proved right. For the thing itself: the show, the family, the truth, the person who's hurting. Here's where it helps this week. Before you call people together, ask what the gathering is for. If the honest answer is to win, it may still happen, and it may even feel good, but in this saying it doesn't last. If the answer is the shared thing, people can disagree hard and still walk out together. The sandal-maker isn't promising calm meetings. He's promising that the purpose decides what's left standing afterward. For heaven's sake endures.
screen: `YOCHANAN, THE SANDAL-MAKER.` · `FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE: IT ENDURES.` · `NOT FOR WINNING. FOR THE THING.` · `ASK WHAT IT'S FOR.` · then, large: `FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE ENDURES.`

segments.voice: Think of one group you're part of that could use getting together: a team, a family, a few friends. Draft a short text inviting them, and before you write when or where, write what it's for in one line, something bigger than anyone in it. Read the line back slowly, and hold off on sending until the sit is done.
screen: `ONE GROUP.` · `WHAT IS IT FOR?` · `WRITE THAT LINE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Gatherings that last. Yochanan the sandal-maker: every gathering for the sake of heaven will endure, and one that isn't, won't.
Pocket this: for heaven's sake endures, even when the meeting is loud. Thirty-four of sixty; see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish study, prayer and community meetings often open by naming their purpose, and some groups dedicate a session l'shem shamayim or in someone's memory before they begin.

fork.setup: your family's planning a reunion, and your two uncles want it at their own houses. you're asked to set up the call. what do you write first?
options: what the reunion is for: getting everyone together, before anyone picks a house.
the pros and cons of each house, so the stronger case can win fairly.
nothing; skip the call so nobody fights and the plan can wait.
fork.reveal: for heaven's sake means for the shared thing. naming the purpose first doesn't end the disagreement, but it's what lets the gathering last.

original.note: Hebrew: for the sake of heaven, for a purpose beyond yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: religious meetings last longer.
what it means: a gathering for something bigger than the people in it endures; one for winning doesn't, whatever it's about.
what a scholar hears: a sage named by his trade, in the same mishnah as the advocate saying, and 'for heaven's sake' is the measure Avot uses again for arguments in chapter five.

chat.says: my two leads aren't speaking. side chats everywhere. calling a cast meeting tmrw so they can hash it out. good?
options: Yes, if you open with what it's for: the show, not who was right.
Yes; let them say everything they're mad about and the strongest side wins.
No; meetings make fights worse. Recast one of them instead.
chat.meaning: Every gathering for the sake of heaven endures. A meeting for the show can hold a loud argument; one for winning doesn't last.

Yochanan HaSandlar.meaning: Yochanan the sandal-maker, a sage of the Mishnah

l'shem shamayim.meaning: for the sake of heaven: for something beyond yourself

mishnah.meaning: one teaching of the Mishnah; here, a single saying of Avot

synagogue.meaning: a Jewish house of prayer and gathering
